The Work, Thought and Torah Legacy of Rabbi Avraham Saba: A Historical, Interpretive and Kabbalistic Study
Introduction and Period of Activity: The Sages of Spain in the Shadow of Rupture and Wandering
The end of the fifteenth century and the beginning of the sixteenth century mark one of the most dramatic and refining chapters in the spiritual history of the Jewish people [cite: 1]. The decrees of 5154 (1391), the Expulsion from Spain in 5252 (1492), and the decrees of forced conversion and baptism in Portugal in 5257 (1497) caused deep upheaval in the world of Iberian Jewry [cite: 2, 3, 4, 5]. Within this reality of physical destruction and theological crisis stands out the spiritual stature of Rabbi Avraham ben Yaakov Saba (5200–5268 / c. 1440–1508), one of the greatest preachers, kabbalists and commentators of the generation of the Expulsion [cite: 2, 3, 4, 6].
The enterprise of Rabbi Avraham Saba is not limited to the composition of an extensive Torah literature, but constitutes a living bridge between the rich homiletic and kabbalistic tradition of Castile and Portugal and the new centers of Torah that arose in North Africa, in the Ottoman Empire and in Europe [cite: 1, 3, 7]. A unique feature, almost without parallel in the annals of Judaism, is the manner in which his works were written: after his original manuscripts were taken from him and torn or buried in the soil of Portugal, he succeeded in reconstructing the main parts of his works from memory alone during his stay in Fez and in Adrianople [cite: 2, 3, 6, 7]. His interpretive and intellectual teaching, which blends plain meaning, homiletics, halakha and mystical secrets, gave theological meaning to suffering and became one of the central sources of inspiration for Renaissance commentators and for the sages who were active in the generations after him [cite: 8, 9, 10, 11].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Life: From Portugal and Lisbon to the Days of the Last Voyage
Rabbi Avraham Saba was born in the city of Zamora in the region of Castile in Spain around the year 5200 (1440) to a distinguished family [cite: 2, 3, 6, 12, 13]. In Castile he acquired his learning from the sages of the generation and began to stand out as a charismatic preacher and spiritual leader who led his community according to the foundations of the revealed and the hidden [cite: 3, 5, 13, 14]. With the publication of the Expulsion decree by the Catholic Monarchs in 5252 (1492), Saba was forced to leave his homeland and set out with his community to neighboring Portugal, where he settled in the city of Guimarães, near Porto [cite: 2, 3, 4, 5, 15]. In Portugal he enjoyed a brief period of five years of relative stability, in which he succeeded in rebuilding his library, preaching before the public of refugees and completing the formulation of his first works [cite: 5, 13].
The period of calm was shattered in 5257 (1497), when Manuel I, king of Portugal, proclaimed decrees of forced conversion and in effect canceled the possibility of leaving the country [cite: 3, 4, 5, 7]. As part of these decrees, the two younger sons of Rabbi Avraham Saba were seized and forcibly baptized [cite: 2, 3, 4, 7]. In an attempt to save his literary work, Saba fled toward Lisbon [cite: 3, 7, 15]. However, following a further royal decree that imposed the death penalty on any Jew found in possession of Hebrew books or ritual objects, he was forced to bury his precious manuscripts – among them his commentaries on the Torah, on the Megillot and on tractate Avot – together with his tefillin, under an olive tree outside the walls of Lisbon [cite: 2, 5, 7, 14, 16, 17].
After the burial of the books Saba was arrested in Lisbon, severely tortured by the authorities and imprisoned for about six months [cite: 2, 3, 7, 14]. When upon his release he tried to dig under the olive tree to retrieve his writings, he was caught again, flogged and put on a rickety ship that sailed to North Africa [cite: 7, 11, 14, 17]. Arriving at the city of Fez in Morocco destitute and broken in body, he fell into a severe illness [cite: 7, 11, 14]. After he recovered, he began a monumental reconstruction enterprise in the course of which he committed his commentaries to writing from his meager memory [cite: 2, 7]. In Fez he lived for about ten years, and afterwards continued his wanderings to Tlemcen in Algeria and to Adrianople in the Ottoman Empire, where he settled and continued to teach and write [cite: 3, 4, 6, 7].
The question of the place of his death and its circumstances has received broad historical and interpretive documentation. The central tradition, mentioned in the book "Divrei Yosef" and quoted at length by the Chida in his book "Shem HaGedolim," relates that in the year 5268 (1508) Saba sailed on a ship on his way to Italy [cite: 3, 6, 7, 11]. During the voyage a severe storm broke out that threatened to sink the ship [cite: 3, 6, 11]. The captain turned to Rabbi Avraham Saba requesting salvation, and Saba promised him that the sea would calm on condition that he swear to bring him to burial in a Jewish grave and not to throw him into the depths [cite: 3, 6, 11]. After Saba prayed and the sea calmed, he died two days later (on the 9th of Tishrei, the eve of Yom Kippur) [cite: 3, 6, 11, 12]. The captain kept his word and brought his body for burial with great honor in the community of Verona in Italy [cite: 3, 6, 7, 11]. Alongside this tradition, there are among some of the sages of the East and historians alternative references that connect his last days or his resting place to Fez in Morocco, as a reflection of his long stay and his enormous influence on the sages of North Africa [cite: 7, 11].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Teachers, His Torah Circle and His Family Ties
The spiritual development of Rabbi Avraham Saba was nurtured directly from the Castilian study hall of the fifteenth century. His foremost teacher was Rabbi Yitzchak de Leon, one of the greatest sages of Spain and its spiritual leaders [cite: 3, 6, 9, 14]. Saba held his teacher in immense admiration and quotes from his novellae and from what he heard from him in the commentary "Tzror HaMor" in the singular: "And the clearest of all is what I heard from the all-embracing sage Rabbi Yitzchak de Leon" [cite: 18]. Rabbi Yitzchak de Leon bequeathed to his student an integrated approach that sees talmudic halakha and the wisdom of the hidden as one organic whole.
The importance of Rabbi Avraham Saba in transmitting the Torah tradition is also expressed in the family and student chain that continued his path. His son, Rabbi Yitzchak Saba, survived the hardships of the Expulsion and settled in the Torah centers of Salonika and Adrianople [cite: 6, 19]. The daughter of Rabbi Yitzchak – the granddaughter of Rabbi Avraham Saba – married our master Rabbi Yosef Karo, author of the "Shulchan Arukh" and the "Beit Yosef" [cite: 6, 19]. This family connection constitutes a vital linking chain: through it the Castilian traditions of homiletics and Kabbalah seeped from the study hall of Saba into the heart of the halakhic and spiritual center that crystallized in Safed in the sixteenth century, and influenced the sages of the generation of ordination and Kabbalah [cite: 1, 6, 19].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Literary Corpus: From Lost Works to Reconstruction from Memory
The literary work of Rabbi Avraham Saba encompasses all the fields of Torah: biblical commentary, the Megillot, tractates of the Sages, halakha, the intentions of prayer and homiletic books [cite: 2, 6, 7, 8]. He was forced to reconstruct most of his works from memory, noting in his introductions and in the course of his commentaries the days of tranquility in Portugal as against the suffering he underwent [cite: 2, 7, 13].
His central and most famous book is "Tzror HaMor" on the Torah [cite: 2, 7, 17]. The work is arranged according to the weekly Torah portions and includes a broad exposition that blends plain meaning, midrashim of the Sages, halakhot and secrets from the Zohar [cite: 2, 8, 9]. The name of the book is derived from the verse "A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me" (Song of Songs 1:13), as an allusion to the bitterness of suffering and to cleaving to God [cite: 20]. The work was greatly admired and was first printed in Venice in 5283 (1523) by the printer Daniel Bomberg, and since then has been printed in many editions and became a foundational book in the study halls [cite: 9, 10, 11, 17].
Another central work is "Eshkol HaKofer," the comprehensive exposition of the five Megillot [cite: 2, 7]. Its parts on the Scroll of Ruth and the Scroll of Esther were printed in stages of the modern period, while fragments of his commentaries on Song of Songs, Lamentations and Ecclesiastes remained in manuscript and were printed in scholarly annotated editions in later years [cite: 7, 21]. Alongside it he composed "Tzror HaChayim" – a kabbalistic-ethical commentary on tractate Avot and on the order of the prayers and blessings, in which he analyzes the structure of prayer according to the system of the sefirot [cite: 4, 6, 7].
Additional works from Saba's pen are mentioned in the Torah and historical literature. The work "Tzror HaKesef," written in his youth in Spain and dealing with the laws of Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and idolatry according to the way of the hidden, was lost in Portugal and he did not succeed in reconstructing it [cite: 3, 6, 7, 13, 14]. Likewise, in bibliographic traditions the work "Eshel Avraham" is attributed to him (a name that also serves as a general designation for his expositions and homilies in manuscript), alongside commentaries on Job and Psalms that were lost in the course of his wanderings [cite: 4, 6, 7]. Recent studies also attribute to him an abridgment of the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol ("Kitzur Semag") [cite: 6].
Title of the Work | Subject and Main Field | Textual State and Style of Reconstruction | Notable Editions and Printings
Tzror HaMor | Comprehensive commentary on the Torah (plain meaning, homiletics, halakha and the hidden) [cite: 2, 8, 9] | Lost in Lisbon, reconstructed from memory in Fez/Adrianople [cite: 2, 3, 7] | Venice 5283 (1523) [cite: 9, 17], Venice 5306 (1546) [cite: 10], Oz VeHadar [cite: 22, 23]
Eshkol HaKofer | Commentary on the Megillot (Ruth, Esther, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes) [cite: 7] | Lost in Portugal, reconstructed from memory in North Africa [cite: 2, 7] | Jerusalem printings, Machon Yerushalayim/Oz VeHadar [cite: 21, 23]
Tzror HaChayim | Commentary on tractate Avot and the intentions of the order of prayer [cite: 4, 7] | Lost, partially reconstructed, preserved in manuscripts [cite: 6, 7] | Yad Ben-Zvi edition, Bnei Brak 5775 [cite: 6, 7]
Tzror HaKesef | Laws of the Days of Awe and idolatry in the way of the hidden [cite: 3, 7, 14] | An early work written in Castile and lost entirely [cite: 7, 13, 14] | Lost [cite: 6, 7, 13]
Eshel Avraham / Additional Commentaries | Homilies, expositions on Scripture (Job, Psalms) and Kitzur Semag [cite: 4, 6, 7] | Some were lost in exile and some were preserved as fragments [cite: 4, 6, 7] | Manuscripts and annotated fragments [cite: 4, 6, 7]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
His Interpretive and Intellectual Teaching: The Relations of Plain Meaning, Homiletics, Halakha and the Hidden
The interpretive method of Rabbi Avraham Saba in the "Tzror HaMor" and in his other works rests on an integrative conception of the biblical text [cite: 2, 8, 9]. Saba sees no contradiction between the revealed and the hidden, but perceives plain meaning as an outer shell and the kabbalistic secret as the inner content that gives plain meaning its spiritual vitality [cite: 2, 9, 24]. In each portion he opens with clarification of textual and structural difficulties, continues with ethical homilies that were originally delivered before the public on Sabbaths and festivals, incorporates halakhic discussions on the customs of prayer and the commandments, and concludes by revealing the mystical substratum from the Zohar [cite: 2, 8, 9, 13, 25].
A central layer in his intellectual teaching is the theology of suffering and destruction [cite: 1, 13]. Saba processes the national and personal crisis of the Expulsion through a prism of the justification of judgment and cosmic clarification [cite: 11, 20]. In his commentary on Song of Songs and on the portions of rebuke, he explains that the suffering that befell Spanish Jewry is not a sign of God's abandonment, but a refining and purifying process of "sufferings of love" [cite: 20]. This position enabled the refugees of the Expulsion to find deep religious meaning in their suffering and to preserve their identity of faith [cite: 1, 11].
With regard to his attitude to medieval philosophy, Saba presents a firm critical position [cite: 1, 26]. He does display mastery of philosophical literature, but argues that exclusive reliance on Aristotelian rationalism failed at the moment of the test of the decrees of forced conversion [cite: 1, 26]. In his view, only simple faith and fundamental mystical apprehension gave the expelled the inner strength to give up their lives for the sanctification of the Name, whereas abstract philosophical engagement weakened standing firm in the test of faith [cite: 1, 7, 26].
Interpretive Dimension | Manner of Application in the Writings of Rabbi Avraham Saba | Sources of Inspiration and Method
Plain-meaning interpretation | Meticulous analysis of the sequence of verses, resolution of syntactic and substantive difficulties [cite: 9, 24] | Classical Spanish interpretation, grammar and the structure of the passage [cite: 8, 18]
Homiletics and ethics | Incorporation of public homilies dealing with the improvement of character traits, faith and the justification of judgment [cite: 8, 13, 20] | Midrashim of the Sages, Tanchuma, Bereshit Rabbah and the Mekhilta [cite: 8, 13, 20]
The halakhic layer | Clarification of the reasons for the commandments, selected laws and customs of prayer and the synagogue [cite: 6, 8, 25] | Babylonian and Jerusalem Talmud, Castilian halakhic rulings [cite: 8, 13, 27]
The hidden and Kabbalah | Exposition of verses and commandments according to the system of the sefirot and the secrets of Kabbalah [cite: 2, 9, 13] | The Zohar, the Kabbalah of Rabbi Yitzchak de Leon [cite: 2, 3, 9, 18]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Influence and Legacy for Generations: From the Sages of Safed to Research and Present-Day Editions
The importance of Rabbi Avraham Saba and his influence on the development of Torah literature are evident over hundreds of years. His work "Tzror HaMor" became a first-rate source for the greatest preachers and kabbalists in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries [cite: 10, 23, 28]. Rabbi Moshe Alshich (the Holy Alshich) in Safed adopted Saba's method of questions and homily, and incorporated ideas from his commentaries into his expositions of Scripture [cite: 10, 23]. Rabbi Yeshayahu HaLevi Horowitz (the Holy Shelah) cites extensively from "Tzror HaMor" in his book "Shnei Luchot HaBrit," in particular on matters of the intentions of the commandments, ethics and the festivals of the year [cite: 23, 28].
In bibliographic and historical literature Saba has been given a place of honor. The Chida in his book "Shem HaGedolim" mentions him with exceeding admiration, preserving the story of his self-sacrifice and the wondrous circumstances of his death [cite: 3, 6, 11]. His commentaries continued to be studied in the study halls of the East and of Europe alike, as a representative model of deep kabbalistic homiletics [cite: 8, 9, 10, 11].
In the modern era his figure has enjoyed a renewed flourishing both in the Torah world and in academic research. In historical and intellectual research, scholars such as Prof. Avraham Gross and Prof. Dov Schwartz analyzed the entirety of his writings, noted his contribution to the shaping of the identity of the expelled from Spain, and presented his spiritual world as a bridge between the Golden Age and the new chapter of Kabbalah in the East [cite: 1, 29, 30]. In parallel, in the Torah world there appeared splendid, corrected and vocalized editions of "Tzror HaMor," "Eshkol HaKofer" and "Tzror HaChayim" by prominent institutes (such as Oz VeHadar, Machon Yerushalayim and Yad Ben-Zvi), which returned his teaching to the heart of study-hall learning [cite: 6, 22, 23, 31].
An especially symbolic and moving event took place in 2017, when a rare copy of the first edition of "Tzror HaMor" (Venice printing, 5283/1523) was returned to Lisbon in Portugal [cite: 17]. This historic closing of a circle, in which Saba's work was restored to the city where he was forced to bury his writings under the olive tree about five hundred years earlier, breathed new life into the story of his self-sacrifice and his Torah legacy [cite: 2, 7, 17].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
Rabbi Avraham Saba, of blessed memory, stands in the annals of Israel as a distinct symbol of spiritual strength, self-sacrifice and creativity that did not yield to the waves of destruction [cite: 2, 7, 11]. From the depths of personal and national loss – the loss of his children, the tearing of his library and the torments of the body – he succeeded in establishing from memory alone a splendid Torah corpus that nourished Jewish thought for generations [cite: 2, 3, 7, 10].
His teaching in the "Tzror HaMor" and in his other works is not merely an interpretive sum, but a living and consoling theology that unites plain meaning and the hidden, judgment and mercy, mourning for the past and firm hope for redemption [cite: 1, 8, 9, 20]. His legacy continues to radiate in the study halls and in research institutes, as a conclusive testimony to the human spirit and to the eternity of the Torah [cite: 1, 17, 23].
